summary: Describes how the Path Computation Element architecture can be applied to determining a sequence of domains for Label Switched Paths across multiple domains in MPLS-TE and GMPLS networks. No single point knows all links and resources in each domain, which causes the problem. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: To plan a trip across many countries, no one has the whole map. This memo shows how helper computers can work out which countries to pass through, in what order.

questions: what is the difference between brpc and hierarchical pce
subtitle: How a parent PCE can pick the sequence of domains for a multi-domain MPLS or GMPLS path without any domain revealing its inside.

tldr.problem: Per-domain computation and Backward-Recursive PCE-based Computation (BRPC) both assume the sequence of domains is known in advance, and nobody sees every domain well enough to choose it.
tldr.mechanism: A parent PCE keeps a map of child domains and the links between them, asks each child PCE for path segments across its own domain, and joins the best segments into an end-to-end path.
tldr.outcome: The RFC is a framework, not a protocol. It lists requirements for PCEP extensions and says the model suits small groups of domains, not the whole Internet.

today: RFC 6805 is an Informational RFC published in November 2012, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It builds on the architecture in RFC 4655.

sections.title: The Problem and Requirements
sections.content:
In a multi-domain network, no single point of path computation knows all the links and resources in every domain. RFC 5152 (per-domain computation) and RFC 5441 (BRPC) both assume the sequence of domains is already known. RFC 6805 asks how to find the best end-to-end path when it is not, for example in optical networks built from sub-domains or in multi-AS settings. A domain here is any collection of network elements within a common sphere of address management or path computation responsibility, such as an IGP area or an Autonomous System.

The RFC sets goals for a solution: it must scale, keep each domain's internal topology confidential, and not rely on exchanging TE information between domains or on one element that knows everything. It should support objectives such as minimum cost or maximum residual bandwidth, capping the number of domains crossed, disallowing domain re-entry, domain diversity (paths that share only the ingress and egress domains), and commercial constraints such as SLAs and peering preferences.

The model is for small groups of domains with limited visibility from the ingress LSR. Applying it to something as large as the Internet is called neither feasible nor desirable. The RFC specifies no protocol extensions.
sections.plainLanguage: Imagine every country keeps its own roads secret. You still want the best route across several countries, so you need a way to choose which countries to cross without anyone showing their full map.

sections.title: Existing PCE Mechanisms
sections.content:
Per-domain path computation (RFC 5152) computes the path domain by domain during signaling, with the entry boundary node of each domain computing its piece. This can give a suboptimal end-to-end path, because the best path in one domain may lead to a poor entry point into the next. If the domain path is not known, the computing entity must guess an exit boundary node, perhaps from the BGP IP shortest path, which does not guarantee bandwidth and may need many crankback attempts. It suits simply connected domains with known interconnection points.

BRPC (RFC 5441) has PCEs cooperate backward from the egress domain. The egress PCE builds a Virtual Shortest Path Tree (VSPT) of optimal paths from its entry boundary nodes to the egress LSR, and each PCE upstream adds its own paths before passing the tree on until the ingress PCE picks the best path. It suits domains with multiple interconnections and no preference among them.

BRPC could be stretched to an unknown domain sequence by sending the request to the egress PCE and passing trees to every neighbor, but the RFC calls this path computation flooding and says it has significant scaling issues.
sections.plainLanguage: Asking each country for directions one at a time can lead you down a bad road. Asking every country at once creates a flood of questions.

sections.title: The Hierarchical PCE Model
sections.content:
A parent PCE holds a domain topology map in which child domains are vertices and their interconnections are links. It knows nothing about what is inside the child domains. Each child domain has at least one child PCE that computes paths across that domain and knows only its own topology and its immediate neighbor domains. For IGP areas, where area border routers sit in both areas, the parent may represent the join as an unconstrained, zero-cost virtual link, which is an implementation matter.

The flow, in outline:

  1. The ingress PCE asks the parent PCE (using PCEP) for a multi-domain path.
  2. The parent selects candidate domain paths from its map and the state of the inter-domain links.
  3. It asks the child PCEs for candidate path segments across their domains, sequentially or in parallel.
  4. It joins the best segments into the end-to-end path and returns it to the child PCE that asked, which passes it to the PCC.

Parent and child PCE may be implemented as a common PCE.
sections.plainLanguage: A boss planner knows which countries touch each other but not what roads are inside them. Each country planner knows its own roads. The boss asks each one for a piece of the trip and glues the best pieces together.

sections.title: Procedures and Protocol Requirements
sections.content:
Objective functions define what optimal means; they state the desired outcome, not the algorithm. They can be requested by the PCC, the ingress domain PCE, or the parent PCE under inter-domain policy. For confidentiality, a PCE may replace a path segment with a path-key (RFC 5520) to hide its content.

Discovery: a child PCE is normally configured with its parent's address, and the parent is configured with its children. Discovering parent-child relationships is not part of the architecture, because advertising or querying PCE locations across domain or provider boundaries is undesirable for security, scaling, commercial and confidentiality reasons. The parent learns domain interconnections from configuration or from child PCEs, which can collect inter-domain TE link information from the IGPs.

Errors: if a child PCE cannot find a path, the parent can cancel the request, relax constraints, or try another candidate domain. If a child does not answer in time, the parent can cancel, try a secondary child PCE in the same domain, or try another domain.

The RFC lists what PCEP extensions would need: a request qualifier asking for a domain sequence only, a way to ask whether a node is in a child's domain, a capability indication for parent PCEs, a way for a child to say it intends to use a parent, a way to report domain connectivity (such as link identifiers, TE properties and the adjacent domain), and unambiguous domain identifiers.
sections.plainLanguage: If one country cannot find a route, the boss can ask again, loosen the rules, or try a different country. Nobody has to show their secret roads, and the boss is told who to talk to by the grown-ups who set it up.

sections.title: A Worked Example
sections.content:
The RFC's example has four domains inside a fifth parent domain. Domain 1 holds the source LSR (S), Domain 3 holds the destination LSR (D), and Domains 2 and 4 sit between them. Each has one child PCE; PCE 5 is the parent.

When the PCC asks PCE 1 for a path to D, PCE 1 sees D is not in its domain and asks PCE 5. PCE 5 determines D is in Domain 3 and, assuming the link BN12-BN22 is not suitable, finds three domain paths: through Domain 2 via BN23 and BN31, through Domain 2 via BN24 and BN32, and through Domain 4 via BN41, BN42 and BN33. It sends edge-to-edge, source-to-edge and edge-to-egress requests to the child PCEs, correlates the replies, adds the inter-domain links, applies policy, selects the best path, and sends it to PCE 1, which forwards it to the PCC.

The RFC notes the child requests need not be sent in parallel or in series; that is an implementation choice.
sections.plainLanguage: The boss planner lists the three possible country-by-country routes, asks each country planner how long its leg would be, and then picks the best combination.

sections.title: Applicability, Management and Security
sections.content:
Hierarchical PCE applies to inter-area and inter-AS MPLS and GMPLS paths, and the RFC shows it matches the ITU ASON hierarchical routing architecture, where a PCE corresponds to a Routing Controller and a routing area to a domain. It also notes that BGP-TE exchange of TE information between ASes makes different assumptions, and that BGP-TE could still feed a PCE's TED.

On management, a child PCE must be configured with its parent's address and be authorized to peer with it, and a parent MUST NOT be assumed to serve unknown children: requests from unauthorized child PCEs should be dropped. A new PCEP MIB module is expected to report parent and child information.

On security, the procedure relies on PCEP and inherits the requirements of RFC 5440. The parent is expected to require full security from child PCEs, and discovery of children by a parent is deliberately not supported. The RFC says multi-domain operation is bound to be a significant security and confidentiality risk when domains belong to different commercial concerns, and that the architecture is designed to isolate domain topology and capability information as far as possible.
sections.plainLanguage: Only planners the boss has approved are allowed to talk to it, and they must use secure channels so no one can fake a route or peek at secret roads.
